chapter_theme: Fate as the force behind wealth, understanding, and pleasure and pain. It reaches even the qualities a person might rely on against it, such as effort and intelligence.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: fate's power over wealth (371-376), over enjoyment and suffering (377-379), and in general (380).

371.reading: A fate of gain produces tireless effort and a fate of loss produces sloth.
371.nuance: Effort is presented as fate's product, not its rival, so the verse removes the usual escape route from fate.

positions.position: Fate itself generates the effort and sloth that help make or lose wealth.
A natural condition, not fate, gives rise to enthusiasm or laziness.

372.reading: A fate of loss makes a person foolish, and a fate of gain, when it arrives, enlarges their understanding.
372.nuance: Intelligence is not a fixed possession here; circumstances of fortune change it.

positions.position: Fate alters even the understanding one is born with.
Natural conditions of ruin and growth produce ignorance and understanding.

373.reading: However many subtle books a person studies, their own understanding still prevails.
373.nuance: The verse doesn't say whose understanding wins or why. The commentators fill that gap differently, and தன் உண்மை அறிவு carries the dispute.

positions.position: The verse concerns one fated to folly, whose fate-given foolishness overrides what study taught.
positions.quote: தன் ஊழான் ஆகிய பேதைமை உணர்வே மேற்படும்

positions.position: Learning may be present, but understanding that comes from fate is stronger.
Natural intelligence rises above study, with no appeal to fate.

374.reading: The world has two distinct natures: being wealthy is one thing, and being wise is another.
374.nuance: Parimelazhagar draws a pointed conclusion: since the wise can be poor and others rich, wealth does not need wisdom as a cause.

375.reading: In making wealth, all that is favourable can turn out badly and all that is unfavourable can turn out well.

positions.position: The 'good' and 'bad' are favourable conditions such as time, place, means and action, which fate overturns.
positions.quote: 'நல்லவை' 'தீயவை' என்பன காலமும், இடனும், கருவியும், தொழிலும் முதலாயவற்றை.

positions.position: Good and bad actions can end in the opposite result, which is simply the natural course.

376.reading: What is not yours will not stay however carefully you guard it, and what is yours will not leave though you throw it away.

positions.position: Possession and loss follow fate, not care or neglect.
positions.quote: பொருள்களின் நிலையும் போக்கும் ஊழினான் ஆவதல்லது, காப்பு இகழ்ச்சிகளான் ஆகா

positions.position: The verse is about what one has a right to, not what fate allots.

377.reading: Even those who have amassed millions can enjoy them only as the one who apportions has apportioned.
377.nuance: வகுத்தான் gives fate a personal agent. This is one of the chapter's clearest points of disagreement about whether a cosmic agent is present.

positions.position: The apportioner is a deity who gives each soul the fruit of its own deeds.
positions.quote: ஓர் உயிர் செய்த வினையின் பயன் பிறிதோர் உயிரின்கண் செல்லாமல் அவ்வுயிர்க்கே வகுத்தலின்

positions.position: What is apportioned is an ordered way of life, and wealth is hard to enjoy without following it.

378.reading: The destitute would renounce the world, if only what they are bound to suffer would pass without afflicting them.
378.nuance: The irony is dry: the poor already lack what renunciation gives up, yet fate withholds even that peace.

positions.position: They could let go of what they lack anyway, but fate's power keeps them suffering through their attitude.
If afflicting feelings left them, they would renounce; the obstacle is psychological.

379.reading: Those who accept things as good when good comes: why do they grieve when it doesn't?
379.nuance: After nine verses on fate's power, this one asks for a response. Fate here is the premise of equanimity.

positions.position: Both are one's own earlier deeds and can't be escaped, so accepting one and resisting the other is unwise.
positions.quote: தாமே முன் செய்து கொண்டமையானும், ஊட்டாது கழியாமையானும்

380.reading: What is stronger than fate? Even when one devises another way, it gets there first.

positions.position: Fate can come through the very plan meant to avert it.
The natural state reasserts itself over artificial arrangements.

links.note: Here effort is fate's product. In 620, effort puts fate behind you. The tension is sharper than one between effort and fate as rivals, because 371 removes effort as an independent force.
Here one's own understanding prevails over study. In 396, knowledge flows in proportion to study.
374 separates wealth and wisdom as different fates, and 400 goes further by calling learning the only true wealth. Read together, they redefine wealth.
In Parimelazhagar's reading both rest on deeds and births: 379 accepts the fruit of past deeds, and 38 stops future births.
